summary: TerraTrend is a web app that lets anyone click any place on Earth and learn whether its climate or environment is changing, why, and where it is heading by 2050. It pulls up to 45 years of live NASA and NOAA data: weather from NASA POWER, air pollution from NASA Giovanni, vegetation from MODIS, sea ice and ocean data from NOAA, and satellite photos from NASA GIBS. Each trend is tested with the Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope. Unusual years are matched to records of 1,841 named storms, 6,197 tornadoes, 5,503 floods, major eruptions and El Niño, and causes are separated into anthropogenic (human causes) and non-anthropogenic (natural causes). A projection model, trained on 4,408 examples from 410 places is used to predict and forecasts each place’s 2026–2050 average. The site also shows the effect on biodiversity, a 3D satellite visualization of the trend, and live global layers for temperature, rain, wind, ocean currents, and El nino watch. The website turns scattered, hard-to-use Earth data into clear answers for any location. This allows people to interact with the website and understand the causes and effects behind many environmental concerns. People protect what they understand, and most cannot read raw climate data. By making the data understandable, people can successfully protect Earth.
details:
How the Project Works

Allows people a place on the 3D globe, type in a location name, or type in coordinates and find out whether the location's climate or environment is changing. The website also displays if the change is statistically real, and the key factors that drive it, and how it will look like in the next 25 years.

Live Data Trend on the Globe: A panel at the bottom left highlights the whole planet with current temperature, rain, sea temperature or the El Niño pattern, and displays animated wind and ocean currents. The El Niño layer additionally outlines the Niño-3.4 region on the Pacific.

TerraTrend Broken Down

1. Pick the location: The visitor spins the globe and clicks a city, a state, a country or any point on land or ocean, or types a name or coordinates into the search box. The site determine what kind of place it is (city, desert, humid tropics, mid-latitude land, polar land, ocean, polar ocean) and offers relevant measurements that the user can choose from.

2. Pick a measurement: There are about twenty measurements that the user can choose from:

  • Air temperature
  • Hottest and coldest monthly temperature
  • Precipitation
  • Soil moisture
  • Humidity
  • Wind
  • Cloud
  • Sunlight
  • Sea surface temperature
  • Sea ice
  • Chlorophyll (ocean plant life)
  • Vegetation greenness (NDVI)
  • Nitrogen dioxide, aerosols (haze, smoke, dust)
  • Sulfur dioxide

3. Understanding the Analysis page: For the chosen place and measurement the site pulls up to 45 years of data live and shows:

  • A headline verdict: Name of the region along with the trend (ex: warming), the rate per decade, the total change, and the p-value of the trend test.
  • The statistical analysis. A pop-up with the full statistics analysis
  • How has it changed: A yearly graph with the line of best fit, its equation, and the unusual years circled and labelled when clicked on.
  • Where is it heading: A projection of the 2026 to 2050 average from a trained model, with an expected range.
  • What pushes it up / What pushes it down: Human and natural causes, each with an explanation and percentages.
  • The years that stand out: Each unusual year is matched to what was happening: El Niño or La Niña, a named hurricane or typhoon, a volcanic eruption, tornado outbreaks, large floods, or unusual local weather.
  • Biodiversity effects: What a change of that kind does to organisms in that type of place.
  • A satellite snapshot: A real NASA satellite photo of the place on a 3D tile, with a year slider and an animation that matches the chosen measurement (ex: raindrops for rain and flames for heat).
  • The mathematical analysis: A pop-up with the full statistics that were run to determine the key statistics.

TerraTrend Architectural Diagram

Explanation: The page fetches open NASA data itself and sends every other request to the Cloudflare relay, which adds the Earthdata token only for NASA Giovanni. The trained models and event catalogues are prepared before launch and travel inside the page; the collector page reaches its data through the same relay.

Data Collection and Sources

Data Collection: The tornado and flood files were downloaded from the agencies and uploaded by hand. The hurricane and typhoon archives and the polar sea-ice records were gathered with the data collector page described below. The training data for the models came from a Python script that asked NASA POWER for 14 measurements at 411 points spread across the world.

Live Data

  1. NASA POWER (MERRA-2 and CERES): Temperature, rain, soil moisture, humidity, wind, cloud, sunlight (monthly, 1981 to now); The browser asks NASA POWER directly
  2. NASA Giovanni / GES DISC (OMI instrument on the Aura satellite): Nitrogen dioxide, aerosols, sulfur dioxide (daily, 2005 to now); Through the Cloudflare relay, which adds the Earthdata token
  3. NOAA ERDDAP data servers (HadISST ice, MODIS Aqua chlorophyll): Sea ice cover (1979 to now) and chlorophyll (2003 to now); Through the relay
  4. NASA ORNL DAAC MODIS service: Vegetation greenness, NDVI (2000 to now); Through the relay, in six-year pieces
  5. NOAA ERDDAP (NCEP global forecast, OISST sea temperature, surface currents): Globe layers: temperature, rain, wind, sea temperature, El Niño pattern, ocean currents; Through the relay, which shrinks each field to a 2° world grid
  6. NASA GIBS (MODIS Terra true colour): Satellite photo for the snapshot; The browser asks GIBS directly

Datasets Built Into the Page

  1. NOAA National Hurricane Center, HURDAT2: Hurricane tracks, Atlantic and eastern Pacific; 432 + 567 storms, 1981 onward
  2. Japan Meteorological Agency best-track archive: Typhoon tracks, western Pacific; 842 storms
  3. NOAA Storm Prediction Center: Tornadoes, United States; 6,197 tornadoes rated EF2 or stronger, 1981 to 2024
  4. Dartmouth Flood Observatory, Global Flood Records: Large floods, worldwide; 5,503 floods, 1985 to 2024
  5. Published climate records: Major volcanic eruptions, El Niño index, volcanic haze index; Small lists inside the model file
  6. Natural Earth: Land colours and borders; One image and the map shapes
  7. NASA Giovanni, downloaded once: Backup city air-quality records; Used only if the relay is unreachable

Machine Learning Models

How Models Were Developed and Shipped:

  1. fetch_training_data.py downloaded the NASA POWER records for 411 points.
  2. train_models.py (Python, scikit-learn) trained and tested the models and wrote the learned numbers to one small file, model.json (about 300 KB).
  3. That file is embedded in the web page. The page re-implements the formulas in JavaScript, so every prediction is computed in the visitor's browser with no server.
  4. Each model's accuracy is shown on the site under "The trained models behind this, and what each one does"

Data Collecter Page:

The collector is a small helper page, separate from the website, that gathers bulk data once so it can be built into the site and used for training.

Why it exists. Some jobs need many records at once: training the sea-ice projection needs decades of ice cover at dozens of polar points, and naming Pacific storms needs two whole storm archives. Fetching those live for every visitor would be slow, and the place where the models were trained could not reach those servers. The relay can, so the collector asks the relay.

How it works.

  1. Open the file in browser and press "Start collecting".
  2. Storm tracks. It asks the relay for the NOAA eastern Pacific hurricane archive and the Japan Meteorological Agency typhoon archive (under a minute).
  3. Sea ice. It asks the relay for the full record at 120 points around the Arctic and Antarctic, four at a time. Points that turn out to be on land are skipped; 95 had ice records.
  4. Vegetation. It asks for NDVI at 30 forests, deserts and farm regions, in six-year pieces because that NASA server is slow.
  5. It saves everything, plus a list of any errors, as one file, etd-collected.json.

What the file was used for. The storm archives added 567 eastern Pacific hurricanes and 842 typhoons to the site's storm catalogue. The sea-ice records trained the sea-ice projection model. The vegetation step is meant to provide a backup for when the NDVI server is down; it has not been completed yet.

Models:

Projection model: Trained in Python (ridge regression)

Purpose: Estimates the 2026 to 2050 average and its expected range

  • Training data. Monthly NASA POWER records from 410 places worldwide for 12 measurements, giving 4,408 examples.
  • How it learned. For each example it saw only 1981 to 2000 and had to predict the average of the following 25 years, 2001 to 2025, which had really happened. This is the same task the site asks of it today.
  • What it learned. For each measurement, how much of a recent straight-line trend usually carries on, plus a typical drift. The formula is: projected change = keep × straight-line change + drift.
  • How it was tested. By holding out whole locations, five rounds, so it was always scored on places it had never seen.
  • How well it does. Its average error was 0.554 (in units of a place's normal year-to-year swing), against 0.816 for assuming no change and 1.154 for extending the straight line. That is 32% better than no change and 52% better than the straight line.
  • The expected range on the graph is the middle 80% of the errors it made in testing.
  • Design choice. Boosted decision trees were also trained and scored 0.530, slightly better. The linear model was kept because its formula can be shown to the visitor and run in a few lines of browser code.
  • Sea ice has its own version, trained on 84 polar-ocean points gathered with the collector page (error 0.912 against 1.010 for no change).
  • Short records. Nitrogen dioxide, aerosols, sulfur dioxide, chlorophyll and NDVI start after 2000, so they cannot be trained this way. They use a pooled model learned from all the other measurements (0.706 against 0.816).

Storm detector: Trained in Python (logistic regression)

Purpose: Flags months whose weather has the fingerprint of a tropical storm

  • Training data. 21,156 months of weather at 86 places around the North Atlantic, June to November, 1984 to 2024.
  • Answer key. NOAA hurricane tracks: 1,069 of those months had a hurricane or strong tropical storm within 200 km.
  • Inputs. Ten measurements for the month (rain, two wind speeds, pressure, cloud, sunlight, two temperatures, two humidity measures), each expressed as how far it was from normal for that place and month.
  • How well it does. On places it had never seen it scores 0.73 on the standard AUC scale, where 0.5 is guessing and 1.0 is perfect. The months it flags are about 7 times more likely than average to have had a storm, but it only catches about 1 storm month in 8.
  • How it is used. As supporting evidence beside the real storm tracks, and only in storm season, at latitudes 8° to 45°, in months with at least 3 mm of rain a day.

Driver model: Fitted live in the browser (multiple regression)

Purpose: Splits the year-to-year story between the long-term trend, El Niño and volcanic haze. Determine the percentages in the "What pushes it up?" and "What pushes it down?" sections.

  • It fits the yearly values to four things at once: a steady trend, the yearly El Niño index, the winter El Niño index and a volcanic haze index.
    • a steady trend over time
    • the yearly El Niño index (Niño-3.4)
    • the winter (December to February) El Niño index

Components that use Statistics and Rules:

Trend tester: Statistics (Mann-Kendall test, Sen slope):
Decides whether the trend is real and how fast it is

Eruption detector: Rule based
Finds days when sulfur dioxide was 5 Dobson Units or more and matches them to known eruptions

Weather matcher: Rule based
Reports which of ten weather measurements were far from normal in a standout year

Cause library: Scientific consensus
Labels a long-term trend as human-caused or natural, for example greenhouse-gas warming for rising temperature

Cloudflare
TerraTrend runs entirely on Cloudflare’s cloud, on the free plan, with no server of its own. A Cloudflare Worker, a small program that runs on Cloudflare’s servers, sits between the website and the data services a browser can’t reach directly. It stores the NASA Earthdata token as an encrypted secret and adds it to requests for NASA Giovanni, so the token never appears in the page and visitors never log in. The same Worker gets past the browser rule that blocks pages from reading other sites’ data, converts every source into one simple format, shrinks the global weather fields to a grid small enough to draw on the globe. The website is also hosted on Cloudflare.
